1.title: ORBIT #001: Great Blue Hole
1.text:
This circular hole is three hundred eighteen meters wide, and no one dug it.

The Great Blue Hole is a three hundred eighteen meter wide marine sinkhole off Belize, formed when sea levels fell during the Quaternary. Jacques Cousteau made it famous as a top scuba diving site. Imagery: Esri, Maxar, Earthstar Geographics. Photos: Jesse Allen; jayhem, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons. Source: Wikipedia.

2.title: ORBIT #002: Vredefort Dome
2.text:
One hundred ten kilometers of hills, and they all circle one small town.

The Vredefort Dome in South Africa is the central uplift of an impact structure formed about 2.023 billion years ago, whose worn-away crater was estimated at 170 to 300 km across. It was added to UNESCO's World Heritage list in 2005. Imagery: Esri, Maxar, Earthstar Geographics. Photos: Júlio Reis (User:Tintazul), Wikimedia Commons. Source: Wikipedia.

3.title: ORBIT #003: Racetrack Playa
3.text:
Rocks up to three hundred twenty kilograms crawl across this dry lake, leaving tracks.

Racetrack Playa is a dry lake in Death Valley National Park, California, where sailing stones weighing up to 320 kg travel across the clay and leave linear tracks. The phenomenon has been documented since 1948. Imagery: Esri, Maxar, Earthstar Geographics. Photos: Dan Duriscoe, for the en:U.S. National P; Lgcharlot, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons. Source: Wikipedia.

4.title: ORBIT #004: Nazca Lines
4.text:
Who scratched over eight hundred miles of lines into this desert?

The Nazca lines are geoglyphs in the soil of the Nazca Desert in southern Peru, made between 500 BC and 500 AD by removing reddish-brown pebbles to expose lighter subsoil. Their combined length is more than 1,300 km, and drones have found several hundred new figures this century. Imagery: Esri, Maxar, Earthstar Geographics. Photos: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons. Source: Wikipedia.
